```{r api-credentials, include=FALSE, echo=FALSE, results='hide', message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
# this chunk is excluded from pdf knitted file and result zip


bsky_handle <- Sys.getenv("BSKY_HANDLE", unset="blank_handle.bsky.social")
bsky_app_password <- Sys.getenv("BSKY_APP_PASSWORD", unset="blank_password")
pds <- "https://bsky.social"  # Default for Bluesky-hosted accounts.
if(need_collect) {
 if(grepl("ENTER_YOUR",bsky_handle)||grepl("ENTER_YOUR",bsky_app_password))
   stop("Enter your own handle and app password in the hidden api-credentials chunk, or set BSKY_HANDLE and BSKY_APP_PASSWORD locally.")
 # University authentication workflow. Token cache remains outside the exported ZIP.
 token <- tryCatch(atrrr::auth(user=bsky_handle,password=bsky_app_password,
   verbose=FALSE,overwrite=TRUE),error=function(e) stop("Authentication failed. Check your own handle and app password."))
 # Create an in-memory session for documented XRPC reads through the account PDS.
 # No authentication response or headers are written to disk or printed.
 login <- httr::POST(paste0(pds,"/xrpc/com.atproto.server.createSession"),
   body=list(identifier=bsky_handle,password=bsky_app_password),encode="json",httr::timeout(60))
 if(httr::status_code(login)!=200L) stop("Unable to create the collection session. Check credentials and PDS host.")
 session <- httr::content(login,as="parsed",simplifyVector=FALSE)
 rm(login,token)
 refresh_session <- function() {
  rr <- httr::POST(paste0(pds,"/xrpc/com.atproto.server.refreshSession"),
   httr::add_headers(Authorization=paste("Bearer",session$refreshJwt)),httr::timeout(60))
  if(httr::status_code(rr)!=200L) stop("Session expired. Knit again to authenticate and resume cached collection.")
  session <<- httr::content(rr,as="parsed",simplifyVector=FALSE)
 }
}
rm(bsky_app_password,bsky_handle)
```

```{r collect-data, include=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
if(need_collect) {
 previous_dir <- getwd()
 tryCatch({
 setwd(work)

library(httr)
library(jsonlite)
assign("%||%", function(x,y) if (is.null(x) || length(x)==0) y else x)
api <- function(endpoint, query, key) {
  path <- file.path("data/raw", paste0(key, ".json"))
  if(file.exists(path)) return(jsonlite::fromJSON(path, simplifyVector=FALSE))
  for(attempt in 1:5) {
    r <- tryCatch(httr::GET(paste0(pds, "/xrpc/", endpoint),
      httr::add_headers(Authorization=paste("Bearer", session$accessJwt),
        `atproto-proxy`="did:web:api.bsky.app#bsky_appview"),
      query=query, httr::timeout(90)), error=function(e) NULL)
    code <- if(is.null(r)) 0L else httr::status_code(r)
    if(code==200L) {
      value <- httr::content(r, as="text", encoding="UTF-8")
      writeLines(value,path,useBytes=TRUE)
      jsonlite::write_json(list(endpoint=endpoint,query=query,status=code,
        collected_at=format(Sys.time(),tz="UTC",usetz=TRUE)),
        sub(".json$",".meta.json",path),auto_unbox=TRUE,pretty=TRUE)
      Sys.sleep(.2)
      return(jsonlite::fromJSON(value,simplifyVector=FALSE))
    }
    if(code==401L) refresh_session()
    if(code %in% c(400L,403L,404L)) stop("API HTTP ",code," at ",endpoint,
      ". Check account access and endpoint availability; no failed request is counted as zero.")
    delay <- if(is.null(r)) NA_real_ else suppressWarnings(as.numeric(httr::headers(r)[["retry-after"]]))
    if(!length(delay)||!is.finite(delay)) delay <- 2^attempt
    Sys.sleep(min(delay,60))
  }
  stop("API request failed after retries at ",endpoint)
}
flatten_post <- function(p) {
  data.frame(uri = p$uri, cid = p$cid %||% "", did = p$author$did,
    handle = p$author$handle, text = p$record$text %||% "",
    created_at = p$record$createdAt, indexed_at = p$indexedAt %||% "",
    reply_count = p$replyCount %||% 0L, like_count = p$likeCount %||% 0L,
    repost_count = p$repostCount %||% 0L, quote_count = p$quoteCount %||% 0L,
    language = paste(unlist(p$record$langs), collapse = "|"),
    parent_uri = p$record$reply$parent$uri %||% "",
    root_uri = p$record$reply$root$uri %||% "", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
posts_list <- list()
coverage <- list()
# Recursively subdivide near-cap intervals. At the minimum interval, follow cursors.
collect_interval <- function(start, end, qi, depth = 0L) {
  iso <- function(x) format(x, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", tz="UTC")
  key <- paste0("interval_", format(start,"%Y%m%dT%H%M%S",tz="UTC"),
    "_", format(end,"%Y%m%dT%H%M%S",tz="UTC"), "_q",qi)
  response <- api("app.bsky.feed.searchPosts",
    list(q=cfg$queries[qi],sort="latest",lang="en",since=iso(start),
         until=iso(end),limit=100L),key)
  batch <- response$posts %||% list()
  if (length(batch)>=90L && as.numeric(difftime(end,start,units="secs"))>60) {
    midpoint <- start + as.numeric(difftime(end,start,units="secs"))/2
    collect_interval(start,midpoint,qi,depth+1L)
    collect_interval(midpoint,end,qi,depth+1L)
  } else {
    cursor <- response$cursor
    seen <- character()
    if(length(batch)>=90L) {
      while(!is.null(cursor) && !cursor %in% seen) {
        seen <- c(seen,cursor)
        if(length(seen)>100L) stop("Search pagination safety limit reached; narrow queries.")
        more <- api("app.bsky.feed.searchPosts",
          list(q=cfg$queries[qi],sort="latest",lang="en",since=iso(start),
               until=iso(end),limit=100L,cursor=cursor),paste0(key,"_p",length(seen)))
        batch <- c(batch,more$posts %||% list())
        cursor <- more$cursor
      }
    }
    posts_list <<- c(posts_list,lapply(batch,flatten_post))
    coverage[[length(coverage)+1L]] <<- data.frame(start=iso(start),end=iso(end),
      query=cfg$queries[qi],retrieved=length(batch),near_cap=!is.null(cursor),
      cursor_returned=!is.null(response$cursor),depth=depth)
  }
}
for (day in seq(cfg$start,cfg$end-1,by="day")) {
  day <- as.Date(day,origin="1970-01-01")
  for (qi in seq_along(cfg$queries)) {
    collect_interval(as.POSIXct(day,tz="UTC"),as.POSIXct(day+1,tz="UTC"),qi)
    cat(as.character(day),qi,"retained rows so far",length(posts_list),"\n")
    flush.console()
  }
}
if(!length(posts_list)) stop("No posts returned for the chosen window and queries.")
raw_posts <- do.call(rbind, posts_list)
posts <- raw_posts[!duplicated(raw_posts$uri), ]
stamp <- as.POSIXct(posts$created_at, format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%OS", tz = "UTC")
topic <- grepl("\\biphone[[:space:]]*(duo|fold)\\b|\\bfoldable[[:space:]]+iphone\\b", posts$text, ignore.case = TRUE, perl = TRUE)
posts <- posts[topic & !is.na(stamp) & as.Date(stamp, tz = "UTC") >= cfg$start &
               as.Date(stamp, tz = "UTC") < cfg$end, ]
posts <- posts[order(posts$created_at, posts$uri), ]
posts <- language_screen(posts)
write.csv(posts,"data/processed/posts_language_screen.csv",row.names=FALSE,fileEncoding="UTF-8")
posts <- posts[posts$language_keep,]

write.csv(posts, "data/processed/posts.csv", row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
write.csv(do.call(rbind, coverage), "data/processed/search_coverage.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(retrieved=nrow(raw_posts), unique=sum(!duplicated(raw_posts$uri)),
  retained=nrow(posts)), "data/processed/collection_counts.csv", row.names = FALSE)
if(nrow(posts)<500) stop("Fewer than 500 eligible posts. Inspect coverage and revise the collection design before submission.")
roots <- posts[posts$parent_uri=="",]
if(nrow(roots)<3) stop("Fewer than three root posts available.")
top <- head(roots[order(-roots$reply_count, -roots$like_count, roots$uri), ], 3)
top$thread <- paste0("T",seq_len(nrow(top)))
top$url <- paste0("https://bsky.app/profile/",top$did,"/post/",sub(".*/","",top$uri))
write.csv(top,"data/processed/top_threads.csv",row.names=FALSE,fileEncoding="UTF-8")
replies <- list()
thread_log <- list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(top))) {
  queue <- top$uri[i]
  visited <- character()
  local_posts <- list()
  blocked <- 0L
  requests <- 0L
  walk <- function(node) {
    if (is.null(node$post)) { blocked <<- blocked+1L; return(invisible(NULL)) }
    p <- node$post
    if (p$uri != top$uri[i]) local_posts[[p$uri]] <<- flatten_post(p)
    children <- node$replies %||% list()
    if ((p$replyCount %||% 0L)>length(children) && !p$uri %in% visited)
      queue <<- unique(c(queue,p$uri))
    for (child in children) walk(child)
  }
  while (length(queue) && requests < cfg$max_thread_requests) {
    uri <- queue[1]
    queue <- queue[-1]
    if (uri %in% visited) next
    visited <- c(visited,uri)
    requests <- requests+1L
    res <- api("app.bsky.feed.getPostThread",
      list(uri=uri,depth=100L,parentHeight=0L),
      paste0("thread_v2_",gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]","_",top$uri[i]),"_",gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]","_",uri)))
    walk(res$thread)
  }
  if (length(local_posts)) {
    frame <- do.call(rbind,local_posts)
    frame$thread <- paste0("T",i)
    replies[[i]] <- frame
  }
  thread_log[[i]] <- data.frame(thread=paste0("T",i),retrieved_replies=length(local_posts),
    advertised_root_reply_count=top$reply_count[i],requests=requests,
    unavailable_nodes=blocked,pending_branches=length(queue))
}
write.csv(do.call(rbind,replies),"data/processed/replies.csv",row.names=FALSE,fileEncoding="UTF-8")
write.csv(do.call(rbind,thread_log),"data/processed/thread_coverage.csv",row.names=FALSE)
activity <- sort(table(posts$did),decreasing=TRUE)
seeds <- data.frame(did=names(activity)[1:3],topic_posts=as.integer(activity[1:3]))
seeds$handle <- posts$handle[match(seeds$did,posts$did)]
write.csv(seeds,"data/processed/seeds.csv",row.names=FALSE)
edges <- list()
actors <- list()
network_log <- list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(seeds))) {
  actors[[seeds$did[i]]] <- data.frame(did=seeds$did[i],handle=seeds$handle[i])
  for (kind in c("followers","follows")) {
    endpoint <- if(kind=="followers") "app.bsky.graph.getFollowers" else "app.bsky.graph.getFollows"
    res <- tryCatch(api(endpoint,list(actor=seeds$did[i],limit=50L),
      paste0("network_v2_",gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]","_",seeds$did[i]),"_",kind)),error=identity)
    if(inherits(res,"error")) {
      network_log[[length(network_log)+1L]] <- data.frame(seed=seeds$handle[i],
        kind=kind,retrieved=0L,more=NA,status=conditionMessage(res))
      next
    }
    nodes <- res[[kind]] %||% list()
    cursor <- res$cursor
    page <- 1L
    page_error <- ""
    while(length(nodes)<50L && !is.null(cursor) && page<10L) {
      page <- page+1L
      next_page <- tryCatch(api(endpoint,
        list(actor=seeds$did[i],limit=50L,cursor=cursor),
        paste0("network_v2_",gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]","_",seeds$did[i]),"_",kind,"_p",page)),error=identity)
      if(inherits(next_page,"error")) {
        page_error <- conditionMessage(next_page)
        break
      }
      nodes <- c(nodes,next_page[[kind]] %||% list())
      nodes <- nodes[!duplicated(vapply(nodes,function(x)x$did,character(1)))]
      if(identical(cursor,next_page$cursor)) break
      cursor <- next_page$cursor
    }
    nodes <- head(nodes,50)
    for(node in nodes) {
      actors[[node$did]] <- data.frame(did=node$did,handle=node$handle)
      edges[[length(edges)+1L]] <- data.frame(
        from=if(kind=="followers") node$did else seeds$did[i],
        to=if(kind=="followers") seeds$did[i] else node$did)
    }
    network_log[[length(network_log)+1L]] <- data.frame(seed=seeds$handle[i],
      kind=kind,retrieved=length(nodes),more=!is.null(cursor),status=if(nzchar(page_error)) page_error else "OK")
  }
}
if(!length(edges)) stop("No network edges retrieved; inspect network access.")
write.csv(unique(do.call(rbind,edges)),"data/processed/edges.csv",row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(do.call(rbind,actors),"data/processed/nodes.csv",row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(do.call(rbind,network_log),"data/processed/network_coverage.csv",row.names=FALSE)
cat("Saved",nrow(posts),"posts and",sum(vapply(replies,nrow,integer(1))),"replies.\n")

 saveRDS(list(completed_at=as.character(Sys.time())),complete)
 },error=function(e) {collection_error <<- conditionMessage(e)},finally=setwd(previous_dir))
}
```

```{r analyse-data, include=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
if(is.null(collection_error)) {
 previous_dir <- getwd()
 tryCatch({
 setwd(work)

library(jsonlite)
library(tm)
library(igraph)
library(cluster)
set.seed(cfg$seed)
read_data <- function(name) read.csv(paste0("data/processed/", name, ".csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
save_table <- function(x, name) write.csv(x, paste0("outputs/", name, ".csv"),
  row.names = FALSE, fileEncoding = "UTF-8")
posts <- read_data("posts")
posts <- posts[order(posts$created_at,posts$uri),]
posts$date <- as.Date(substr(posts$created_at, 1, 10))
posts$period <- factor(ifelse(posts$date < cfg$event, "Before", "After"),
                      levels = c("Before", "After"))
# Classification concerns the foldable iPhone, not any amount in its post.
# Conservative clause-level attribution; ambiguous cases are explicitly queued.
price_label <- function(text) {
 text <- tolower(gsub("https?://[^[:space:]]+", " ", text, perl=TRUE))
 clauses <- unlist(strsplit(text,"(?<=[.!?;])\\s+|[\\r\\n]+",perl=TRUE))
 target <- "\\biphone\\s*(duo|fold)\\b|\\bfoldable\\s+iphone\\b"
 cue <- "\\b(pric(e[sd]?|ing)|cost(s|ly)?|expensive|cheap(er|est)?|afford(able|ability)?|unaffordable|overpriced|financing|instalments?|installments?|monthly payments?|value for money|worth (it|the price))\\b|[$£€]\\s*[0-9]"
 unrelated <- "\\b(polymarket|prediction.market|price target|stock|shares?|funding|fundrais[a-z]*|roi|market cap|valuation)\\b"
 other <- "\\b(iphone\\s*[0-9]*\\s*(pro|max|air)|airpods|apple watch|galaxy|samsung|xiaomi)\\b"
 direct <- paste0("(",target,")\\s+(?:(?:will|reportedly|is|expected|to|could|may|be)\\s+){0,6}(starts? (at|from)|begins? at|costs?|priced? (at|from)|[$£€]\\s*[0-9])")
 has <- function(pattern,x) grepl(pattern,x,perl=TRUE)
 t <- has(target,clauses); c <- has(cue,clauses)
 near <- has(paste0("(",target,").{0,140}(",cue,")|(",cue,").{0,140}(",target,")"),clauses)
 competing <- has(unrelated,clauses) | (has(other,clauses) & !has(direct,clauses))
 positive <- any(t & c & near & !competing)
 ambiguous <- any(c) && (!positive || any(t & c & competing))
 reason <- if(positive) "target_price_same_clause" else if(any(t & c & competing))
   "competing_financial_or_product_context" else if(any(c)) "price_not_clearly_attributed_to_target" else "no_price_cue"
 list(label=positive,review=ambiguous,reason=reason)
}
classified <- lapply(posts$text,price_label)
posts$rule_label <- vapply(classified,`[[`,logical(1),"label")
posts$needs_context_review <- vapply(classified,`[[`,logical(1),"review")
posts$classification_reason <- vapply(classified,`[[`,character(1),"reason")
posts$subtopic <- posts$rule_label
# Do not silently claim that dictionary labels have been validated.
# An optional manual override file applies ONLY explicit labels for matching URIs.
override_path <- file.path(work,"manual_price_overrides.csv")
if(file.exists(override_path)) {
 overrides <- read.csv(override_path,stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
```

\newpage

# Study design

In this study, public Bluesky discussion around the iPhone Duo announcement on 9 September 2026 is analyzed [@apple2026].  The topic of discussion include pricing aspects such as quoted prices, perceived costs, the ability to buy the phone without suffering a big financial burden, and the overall value-for-money aspect of the new smartphone. This article also conducts comparative analysis to see how many relevant posts were made in the period before and after announcement, provides daily summary of discussions count, analyses the responses to the most discussed posts, and visualizes local follows network [@wsu2026].

The observed periods are from 26 August to 8 September 2026 and from 9 September to 22 September 2026, determined according to UTC time. The day of occurrence is included in the second observation period; hence, the posts made before the product announcement are considered to belong to the second period.

## Window rationale

The rise and fall of collective attention happens very quickly which implies that an event-oriented period can be observed [@lorenz2019]. The design consideration is the 14-day period of the past and of the future which allows for two whole weekly cycles thus not overlapping with more remote events. It is possible to conduct the analysis by one week-long periods which serve the sensitivity test. Neither of the designs suffers from the presence of simultaneous news, expectations, or selection bias.

## Collection and reproducibility

Authenticated requests read are based on the protocol provided in the university authentication manual. The search involves both official name and usual names of the foldable iphone as well as the request in English, the second literal relevancy check, and the independent detection of the language used in the text. All the ambiguous requests “iPhone Ultra” are omitted from the search. The two periods are characterized by the application of the same principles.

The research retains significant post URIs as well as timestamps for creation. The original responses have been saved in cache, which means that every subsequent knit will give the collection again. Only those posts that have been found as written in English through CLD3 technology are kept [@cld3];  all the posts that were not clear or written in a different language are sent for analysis. The determination might be wrong if a message is short and written in several languages. The search could be incomplete as well. The search might not contain all posts from a platform. The engagement, replies, and following were collected at the time of collection, which does not mean they were obtained on the announcement day [@bluesky2026].

```{r run-status, results='asis'}
if(!analysis_ok) {
 cat("**Run incomplete.** ",if(!is.null(collection_error)) collection_error else analysis_error,
 "\n\nAvailable diagnostic outputs have been exported. No missing results are imputed. Correct the reported issue before submission.\n",sep="")
} else {
 knitr::kable(data.frame(Posts=s$n_posts,Authors=s$n_authors,Before=s$n_before,After=s$n_after),caption="Retained study sample.") |> print()
}
```

# Question 1: Price, affordability and temporal trends

## Q1(a): Subtopic classification

A clause-level requirement says that the phrase about either price or affordability must be seen near the direct reference to the foldable iPhone. Financial market situations and fundraising are excluded. Mentions of the competitors should be more informative as well. Using purchase language is not enough. In unclear cases, the issues are solved based on context.

A validation sample is created using a maximum of twenty posts from each time stratum (not including data already used in prior reviews). The label sheet is separate from predictions. The field `manual_label` must be populated with 1 for price/affordability issues and 0 otherwise; justifications are required. Completed labels allow calculation of weighted precision and recall for an eligible validation sample (excluding data used already); the inequality of stratum sampling will be considered. The labels are transformed into an evaluation set, which means that they will not be directly utilized for correcting rules. If the rules will be changed based on the newly obtained sample, then this sample is considered as development data, and a new independent evaluation sample is needed. 


```{r validation-status, eval=analysis_ok}
tbl("outputs/validation_status.csv",caption="Independent classification review status.")
if(file.exists(file.path(work,"outputs/validation_metrics.csv")) && validation_complete)
 tbl("outputs/validation_metrics.csv",digits=4)
```


```{r q1a, eval=analysis_ok}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Period=rownames(a$table),Other=as.integer(a$table[,1]),
 Price_affordability=as.integer(a$table[,2]),Total=rowSums(a$table),
 Share=a$table[,2]/rowSums(a$table)),digits=4,caption="Subtopic counts and proportions.")
```

### Observed price and affordability discussion


The retained dataset contains 4,199 posts from 2,667 profiles. The price/affordability issue occurred in 26 of 238 posts recorded in the pre-period (10.92%) and 474 of 3,961 posts compiled after (11.97%). The increase is 1.04%. Although the number of posts related to price has considerably increased, the general volume of discussion grew simultaneously, thus the ratio can answer the raised research question more effectively than only raw numbers of price-related posts.

The presented findings are not verified population rates, but rather are rule-based estimations. The validation document sent exhibits a total of 80 sampled posts, but there are no labels complete. The attribution approach covers certain examples that are unrelated to price, however, the independent values of precision and recall are not clear yet. The linguistic filter alters the corpus so it is unreasonable to say that the improvements from previous results are solely due to the better price classification.

## Q1(b): Pearson chi-square test

The null hypothesis states that the period and the status regarding subtopic are in an independent relationship. The alternative is an association. The test uses $E_{ij}=R_iC_j/N$ and $\chi^2=\sum (O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2/E_{ij}$, without Yates' correction [@rchi2026]. The severity of the effect can be assessed by Cramér's $V=\sqrt{\chi^2/n}$ for the table with two by two values. Non-significant results do not imply any sort of equality.

```{r q1b, eval=analysis_ok}
knitr::kable(a$chi$expected,digits=2,caption="Expected counts.")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Chi_square=s$chi,p_value=s$p,Cramers_V=s$cramers_v,
 Minimum_expected=s$expected_min,Monte_Carlo_p=s$p_monte_carlo),digits=5)
```

### Statistical interpretation

The results of the Pearson test are chi-square=0.2325 and p=0.6297. The null hypothesis is accepted at the 5% threshold, which means that the result is not indicative of the connection between period and classified price talk. The Cramér’s value equals 0.0074, meaning that the correlation that has been observed is very weak, and minimum expected count is 28.34, so the usual worry of low expected cells does not exist [@rchi2026].

The Monte Carlo comparison does not correlate with independence as well. Sensitivity analysis has confirmed that using authors’ first posts does not change things (p = 0.6483) as well as deduplication of exact texts (p = 0.3283). They still have to deal with search-and-selection bias, dependency, and classification error. The sample size has decreased, so the estimates are less precise.

## Q1(c): Twitter-style chi-square score

Module 9 treats historical frequencies as expected values. To accommodate unequal period totals, let $p_B=X/N_B$, $E_A=N_Ap_B$, and compute
\[
S_T=\frac{(Y-E_A)^2}{E_A}+\frac{(N_A-Y-N_A(1-p_B))^2}{N_A(1-p_B)}.
\]
With equal totals for periods, it leads to the formula mentioned above. Pearson assumes that there will be some value for expected proportions; however, his formula implies that the historical number of proportion is fixed and its estimation error is disregarded. This is not correction by Yates [@wsumodules2026].

```{r q1c, eval=analysis_ok}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Pearson=s$chi,Twitter_style=s$twitter_score),digits=5)
```

## Q1(d): Daily linear regression

For the 28 daily observations, fit $Y_t=\alpha+\beta t+\varepsilon_t$, where $t=0$ on the first observation day. All calendar days are represented. A zero is assigned only within a successfully completed collection.

```{r q1d-plot, eval=analysis_ok, fig.cap='Daily retrieved topic posts, fitted trend and announcement date.'}
fig("outputs/daily_counts.png")
```
```{r q1d-results, eval=analysis_ok}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Slope=s$slope,CI_lower=s$slope_ci[1],CI_upper=s$slope_ci[2],
 p_value=s$slope_p,R_squared=s$r_squared),digits=5)
```

### Temporal interpretation

The most posts were on September 9: 1,720, which is almost 41% of the selected dataset. This coincides with increased attention to the announcement day, although the design cannot separate the announcement from concurrent coverage [@lorenz2019].

The slope was found to be equal to 4.96 posts a day. The confidence interval is 95% somewhere between -12.29 and 22.21, p = 0.5596, and R-squared = 0.0133. Hence, the straight line can explain only 1.33% of variation in the daily data. Note that the weak fit of the model does not necessarily mean that no spike occurred: the constant trend does not suit for a sudden event followed by a decline, and further predictions cannot be made. 

## Q1(e): Limitations and sensitivity

Count data over days show rapid spikes, non-homogeneous variance, and serial correlation. A straight line is used to average those trends and cannot give a causal event impact determination. The searching process isn’t a probability sampling procedure, the authors repeat the publications thus violates a simple independence principle, and a period before the event already has rumors.

```{r q1e, eval=analysis_ok, fig.cap='Regression residual and normal-quantile diagnostics.'}
fig("outputs/regression_diagnostics.png")
tbl("outputs/window_sensitivity.csv",digits=5,caption="Seven- and fourteen-day comparisons.")
```

### Observation-window sensitivity

Seven-day comparison changes from 12.78% beforehand to 13.25% after (an increase by 0.47 percentage point) with p = 0.8745. The fourteen-day window gives an increase of 1.04 percentage points with p = 0.6297. Both are non-significant. Similarity of the results from these two periods is good in this data but doesn’t provide justification for the model or prove absence of the real effect.

# Question 2: Threads and word frequencies

## Q2(a): Top three root posts

Choose root posts by reply count descending; ties are broke by likes and URI. The selection refers to retrieved eligible posts, not to all posts on Bluesky. Replies collected are stated as available nested descendants; blocked/deleted nodes and pending branches are considered as materials. Replies are collected in the current time without limiting them to the event window.

```{r q2a, eval=analysis_ok, results='asis'}
top <- read.csv(asset("data/processed/top_threads.csv"),check.names=FALSE)
for(i in seq_len(nrow(top))) {
 cat("\n\n**",top$thread[i],"**\n\nAccount: `",top$handle[i],"`\n\n",sep="")
 print(knitr::kable(data.frame(Replies=top$reply_count[i],Likes=top$like_count[i],Reposts=top$repost_count[i])))
 # Verbatim text keeps markdown/LaTeX syntax in posts from being executed.
 safe <- iconv(top$text[i], from="UTF-8", to="ASCII//TRANSLIT", sub="?")
 safe <- gsub("`","'",safe,fixed=TRUE)
 cat("\n\n~~~~text\n",safe,"\n~~~~\n\n[Original post](",top$url[i],")\n",sep="")
}
```

## Q2(b): Top fifteen words per thread

Lowercase conversion and removal of hyperlinks, tags, punctuation marks, digits and the English stop words except for “no”, “not” and “nor”; all tokens with product names are filtered. No stemming of words occurs. Replies which have been identified as English will be retained. Replies whose status is uncertain are discarded along with replies in other languages. Although it results in discarding valid short replies in English, the language screening table is sometimes needed.
Frequencies are calculated based on the number of occurrences of the token in question but they do not indicate sentiment [@feinerer2008; @manning2008].

```{r q2b, eval=analysis_ok, fig.cap='Fifteen most frequent retained words in each thread.'}
fig("outputs/thread_terms.png")
tbl("outputs/top15_terms.csv",caption="Thread word frequencies.")
```

## Q2(c): Comparison of discussion themes

### Comparison of the three discussions

**Thread 1: interface humour and community references.** The content suggests the supposed leak of a Bluesky project design. The retained forms of the response contain 18 words “people” and “yelling” and 15 “jerry”. The analysis of replies reveals jokes about “Jerry” button and yelling, about the device’s functions. This thread demonstrates humour rather than discussion of affordability of the device.

**Thread 2: expected price and purchase justification.** The original post cites a projected price of over $2,000. Responses question the expenditure by drawing comparisons with PCs and rival smartphones, as well as looking at alternative phones. Others argue that it's not as prohibitive if installment arrangements are taken into account, thus exhibiting conflicting attitudes towards the new phone.

**Thread 3: announced price, product comparisons and brand disagreement.** The root mentions a price of $1,999 dollars. In the thread, *Apple* is mentioned 17 times, the term *phone* is used 11 times, the term *fold* appears 10 times, and the name *Samsung* is written 8 times. The participants in the thread compare different foldable devices, talk about the software used in these devices, hardware specifications, and discuss the attitude of people towards the Apple brand. Some discussions in the threads do not address the price question, but talk about innovation and brand loyalty.

Word frequencies across the threads can be informative, but their meaning cannot be determined without the context of the replies since it is impossible to identify jokes, disagreements or approval  [@manning2008]. The three popular roots chosen are not representative of the entire population or all possible customers.

# Question 3: TF-IDF and clustering

## Q3(a): Document representation

Each reply is a document. Terms occurring in fewer than two documents are removed. We use $w_{dt}=\log(1+tf_{dt})\log(N/df_t)$ and normalise nonzero document vectors to unit length. The zero-complex is ruled out of consideration and judgement. In contrast, the squared Euclidean distance in regards to unit vectors is equal to two times the value of the cosine dissimilarity concept [@wsumodules2026; @manning2008].

```{r q3a, eval=analysis_ok}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Retrieved_replies=s$replies_total,Language_eligible=s$eligible_replies,
 Zero_vectors=s$zero_vectors,Clustered_documents=s$cluster_n,Terms=s$vocabulary))
```

## Q3(b): Selecting the number of clusters

Cluster analysis through K-means with a normalised term set is carried out with 50 iterations per candidate K along with constant seeds. The combination of the within-cluster sum-of-squares parameter is used in order to indicate the compactness. Elbow refers to K whose distance between the normalised WSS and the direct line joining the points is maximal. The silhouette provides another parameter for evaluation; though both methods do not guarantee success in achieving clusters [@rkmeans2026; @rousseeuw1987].

```{r q3b, eval=analysis_ok, fig.cap='WSS elbow and silhouette diagnostics.'}
fig("outputs/cluster_selection.png")
tbl("outputs/cluster_selection.csv",digits=4)
```

## Q3(c–d): Clusters and two-dimensional display

In classical multidimensional scaling, one can observe the Euclidean distances. Different clusters are marked with different colours, while various shapes are used to depict threads; clustering is performed prior to the projection [@rmds2026].

```{r q3cd, eval=analysis_ok, fig.cap='MDS projection of the clustered reply vectors.'}
fig("outputs/clusters_2d.png")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Selected_K=s$k,Mean_silhouette=s$mean_silhouette,
 Positive_eigenvalue_fraction_2D=s$mds_gof),digits=5)
```

## Q3(e): Comparison with thread membership

```{r q3e, eval=analysis_ok}
tbl("outputs/cluster_thread_table.csv")
tbl("outputs/cluster_terms.csv",digits=4,caption="Highest mean-weight terms within clusters.")
purity <- sum(apply(a$cross,1,max))/sum(a$cross)
baseline <- max(colSums(a$cross))/sum(a$cross)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Purity=purity,Majority_thread_baseline=baseline,
 Adjusted_Rand_index=s$ari),digits=5)
```

### Interpretation of cluster structure

A total of 192 replies of 258 were included as a result of language filtering, leading to 178 texts and 234 terms after erasing 14 zero vectors. The elbow method resulted in five clusters with 102, 11, 26, 20 and 19 sizes. The first cluster includes 57.3% of texts and most of the interacting terms and indicates a big heterogeneous group.

While clusters 2 and 5 contain the vocabulary typical of the first thread: *jerry/button* and *people/yelling/caps*. Additionally, cluster 3 comprises *phone/Samsung/fold* and combines three threads. *Apple*, extensive evaluative vocabulary, and references to prices are in cluster 4 based on threads 2 and 3.
The above attempts denote preliminary vocabulary description and no audience segmentation.

The mean silhouette is equal to 0.0204 showing low segregation [@rousseeuw1987]. The two-dimensional projection of the results includes only 4.88% of relevant variance indicating that its visual distances are poor [@rmds2026].  The purity is equal to 55.62% against 44.38% of majority-thread baseline, and adjusted Rand index is equal to 0.0348. Some elements of specific vocabulary have been found but there is a general low degree of correlation. Thread names appear not to have independent semantic ground truth.

# Question 4: Follows network

## Q4(a): Most active accounts

The three threads are the ones that retained the most posts on the topic as revealed by the constant DIDs as the volume of posting can hardly be an indicator of human interaction and power.

```{r q4a, eval=analysis_ok}
tbl("data/processed/seeds.csv",caption="Most active sampled accounts.")
```

## Q4(b): Network construction

For each seed, obtain a maximum of 50 followers and followed accounts, process as needed, check for identical accounts before capping. An edge exists from follower to followed account. This is the network of observed seed-unrelated edges; the unobserved links of possible accounts are not known not to exist. This is a restricted local network not a global platform.

```{r q4b, eval=analysis_ok, fig.cap='Observed directed follows network; highlighted nodes are the three seeds.'}
fig("outputs/network.png")
tbl("data/processed/network_coverage.csv",caption="Network collection coverage.")
```

## Q4(c): Degree and PageRank

Incoming follows have in-degree counts and outgoing follows have out-degree counts. In PageRank, the sum of incoming links multiplied by the weight of the sources and outgoing link distribution comes under consideration, damping value being 0.85 [@freeman1979; @igraph2026]. The seed choice and capped sampling practices influence all metrics.

```{r q4c, eval=analysis_ok}
central <- a$centrality
for(metric in c("in_degree","out_degree","pagerank")) {
 ranked <- central[order(-central[[metric]],central$handle),c("handle","in_degree","out_degree","pagerank")]
 print(knitr::kable(head(ranked,10),digits=5,caption=paste("Top accounts by",metric)))
}
```

### Interpretation of centrality

The graph contains 194 accounts and 207 edges in one weakly connected component. The seeds are technology-news (69 topic postings), radionizza (50), and appleinsider (45). All the seeds have in-degree 50, indicating the count cap and in no measure popularity on the global platform level.

Radionizza has been found to possess the highest observed out-degree (50) and the highest combined degree (100). The highest PageRank is recorded for Appleinsider's (0.10274) followed by radionizza (0.09676) and technology-news (0.09397). This indicates that the method of counting links and estimating weights of incoming links from their origin does not always lead to identical results [@igraph2026].

The account of bsky.app takes fourth place (0.08227) with only one counted incoming edge. The only counted outgoing follow from technology-news points at bsky.app, which shows the importance of linking sources and the way PageRank can be obtained. These are the properties of the graph obtained. However, the absence of non-seed connections, restriction of followers, and choice of very active seeds do not allow making a statement about global position [@freeman1979].

# Synthesis and limitations

### Overall findings

While the same announcement leads to a disproportionate surge in discussion, there has been a small change in classified price/affordability shares. Neither the two-week nor the one-week tests show any evidence of cross-correlation at the 0.05 level. The conclusions are based on the untested classifier and the chosen search corpus. Thus, they do not speak about sales, demand, or causality.

Analysis of threads shows three types of discussions: conversations about community humour, price justification, and comparisons of brands/products. The clustering approach shows some unique vocabulary but does not provide any strong support for particular groups. The network analysis results indicate differences in terms of activity, degree, and PageRank in the sample. The important conclusion is that high volume of discussions about launches cannot be equated with acceptance of the price/affordability aspect by the public.

The findings of this report have a number of limitations resulting from query parameters, language filtering, non-random search retrieval, repeated contributors, and retrospective engagement snapshots. The three leading threads do not necessarily capture all discourse. A label dictionary may not be able to detect sarcasm and implicit issues regarding affordability. Clustering can cause instability in the case of short replies. A two-week design reflects association around an announcement and does not demonstrate causal relationships or consumer demand.
